passage:
My younger brother Sachin used to lead the evening prayer at home, ringing the little bell before anyone else. Since our grandmother died in the spring, he stands at the back with his lips barely moving.

Last week he sat down beside me on the balcony. "Chandrika, I say the words and they feel empty. Does anyone listen?" I had no answer, and I told him so. He didn't seem upset with me. He just nodded.

Since then he has been reading widely, old commentaries and a sceptic's book side by side, and on Sundays he meets an old college professor for tea. He hasn't stopped praying, and he doesn't claim to believe either. I can't tell what is going on inside him. I only know he seems to be asking honestly.

qa.q: Who does Sachin meet on Sundays?
qa.a: Sachin meets an old college professor for tea on Sundays.

qa.q: What might Sachin be feeling when the words of prayer seem empty?
qa.a: Sachin seems doubtful and unsure whether anyone listens, since he asked Chandrika directly and started reading both sides, though Chandrika cannot be sure what is inside him.
Keep listening without pushing belief or disbelief, as Chandrika did by admitting there was no answer, and welcome the wide reading and the Sunday talks.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see Sachin's questions?
qa.a: Chandrika cannot tell what is going on inside Sachin but sees honest asking rather than a rejection of the family.

grounding: After a loss, prayer feels empty to Sachin, who asks questions, reads widely and talks with a thoughtful person without forcing belief or disbelief.
